newsitem.title: ITALY: Telescopes out for signs BTP supernova to fade.
newsitem.headline: Telescopes out for signs BTP supernova to fade.

text.p: Dazzling Italian debt markets may have a little further to fly, but the up-up-and-away rally of recent months is becoming dizzying and a correction may be due, traders said on Wednesday.

Dealers say although the market has renewed record highs for days, volumes are starting to fade and, with the year end approaching, the Italian bond (BTP) futures buoyancy, while unlikely to collapse, has the potential to deflate a few points.
Traders say the market has scope to climb a point or point and a half from the 128.58 record high set on Wednesday.
"But the market is holding substantial long positions. The world and his mother is in this market and it's a bit worrying," said Jonathan York, broker at Cater Allen Futures in London.
Another broker said general funds were now underweight or neutral on high yielders but hedge funds remained overweight.

"It's a potentially interesting situation because they're not in for the long haul. They're in to make money and if sentiment changes, those funds are the ones that get out very quickly and there's nobody else holding the market," she said.
Few yet saw a massive correction in the near future although prolonged selling was not ruled out next year as Italy struggles to meet goals for European economic convergence.
Instead, traders said given the aggression of the BTP rally, the market could sustain a pullback of a couple of points without serious harm.

Dealers note much BTP-positive news is priced in, like the expected return of the lira to Europe's exchange rate mechanism and an expected inflation slowdown to about 2.6 percent this month, which, many believe, would allow a Bank of Italy easing.
But one broker said the downside threat exists if a rate cut does not happen, or not as soon as the market has imagined.

Others said risk came from a retracement in other bonds which would hit BTPs as well. This might be sparkled by a faster than expected change in Germany's rate outlook or else from Italian political problems.

Sally Wilkinson, international economist at UBS in London, said: "Italy may see problems with constitutional reform next year. Or it could be that it becomes much clearer how decisions on EMU are going to taken."

Since September the front month BTP futures contract has stormed 13 points up with only one pause for breath at 123 during October. Investors buying in January this year would have seen a rally from 108.
The spread of the benchmark 10-year Btp over the Bund has wound in from more than 300 basis points in August and now stands at 178 with expectations it could track Spain in to 150.

Economists argue foreign investors are not fooled by what they call the Rome government's window-dressing on its budget deficit targets for next year and say in reality few believe Italy will make it to European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
"Italy's taking a gamble and it may just work because the more the financial markets believe it, the more likely they are to get there because of the interest savings," Wilkinson said.
"But if it (the spread) does unwind it will do so very aggressively," she said. She expected next year would see the bond spread back at 275 on an over-correction before stabilising above 200.

Luca Jellinek, bond strategist at Paribas in London, said while overseas investors did not believe Italy would make the EMU deadline, nevertheless existing market confidence could be shaken next year as 1996 and 1997 deficit data came out.
"They'll overshoot the target. Once the numbers start coming, the proof is in the pudding," he said.
--Milan bureau +392 66129507
